To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
K(Ca)(+) channels in the BTB are a novel target for the enhancement of drug delivery to brain.

bradykinin and nitric oxide (via cGMP) activate calcium-dependent potassium (BK) channels in brain tumor capillary cells, which leads to an increase in pinocytotic activity and an enhanced drug delivery into brain tumors.

bradykinin and calcium-activated potassium (K(CA)) channels enhance the permeability of the blood-brain tumor (BTB) barrier to macromolecules by increasing the rate of vesicular transport of these macromolecules across the BTB.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel strategies to enhance drug delivery to the brain tumors.
the development of a novel approach to increase BTB permeability and drug delivery to brain malignancy.

the regulation of BTB by K(Ca) and NO/cGMP signaling and provides new insights into the molecular mechanism of the BTB permeability regulation and the potential use of these signaling pathways for the selective drug delivery to the brain tumor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the K(Ca) agonists, BK and NS-1919, increase BTB permeability in brain tumors by increasing the formation of pinocytic vesicles in the tumor capillary endothelium and glioma cells.
the BK-induced increase in BTB permeability is a result of the opening of K(Ca)-channels in the tumor capillary endothelial cells and tumor cells.

the present study has demonstrated the involvement of K(Ca)-mediated mechanisms in the regulation of BTB and that the activation of these channels may be a promising strategy for the enhancement of selective drug transport across the BTB.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the BTB is regulated by the K(Ca) ion channel, which is a convergence point for a number of signaling pathways that regulate the BTB.
BK, sGC, and NO donors can be used to enhance BTB permeability to brain tumor by activating K(Ca) and Ca(2+)-dependent vesicular transport.

the BK-induced increase of BTB permeation is a result of the BK-induced increase in K(Ca) currents, the BK-induced increase NO/cGMP production, and the BK-induced increase formation of transport vesicles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have demonstrated that the blood-brain tumor barriers (BTB) can be opened by the activation of potassium channels.
the BTB is not a passive structure but a highly active structure that can be regulated by various agents.
K(Ca)-channel-mediated BTB permeabilization may provide a therapeutic window for the delivery of anticancer drugs to brain tumors.
